title: Unit 7 — Humour
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Why a Course in Language Needs a Course in Laughter

Humour is the hardest thing to do in a second language and the fastest way to sound native in it: a pun lands only if you hear the double meaning, irony only if you catch the gap between said and meant. This unit names the species of comedy, trains you to analyse why something is funny (examiners ask exactly this), and equips your own writing with the devices — exaggeration, timing, understatement — that make narratives and essays memorable.

## 2. Fundamental Conceptual Understanding — What Makes Things Funny

### 2.1 The machinery of laughter: incongruity and release

The dominant theory is worth quoting in any analysis: humour arises from **incongruity** — two frames colliding (a priest slipping on ice, a formal letter with a spelling howler) — and from **release**, the sudden discharge of tension when the punchline resolves the collision safely. Superiority theories (we laugh at misfortune that spares us) and relief theories (laughter vents anxiety) explain the rest. A strong answer names the theory, then points to the exact line where the two frames meet.

### 2.2 The species of humour — learn to name them

- **Slapstick:** physical comedy — the banana peel, the cream pie; universal, needs no language.
- **Pun / wordplay:** one sound, two meanings — "Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana."
- **Irony:** meaning the opposite of what you say; the audience must know the truth to get it.
- **Sarcasm:** irony with a bite, aimed at a person — funny to allies, wounding to targets.
- **Satire:** organised irony aimed at institutions and vices, meant to reform, not just sting — cartoons mocking corruption are satire; mocking a classmate is not.
- **Parody:** imitating a style to comic effect — a news bulletin about a lazy student delivered in solemn anchor-speak.
- **Deadpan:** the funnier the material, the flatter the delivery; the gap does the work.
- **Self-deprecation:** aiming the joke at yourself — the safest and most likeable humour in any culture.

### 2.3 Humour across cultures (and what travels badly)

Physical comedy crosses borders; wordplay rarely does (it lives in the language's particular seams). Formality rules differ: teasing elders is warm in some circles, disrespectful in others — in much of Nepali society, humour flows downward in age more safely than upward. The exam-generalisable point: humour is **culturally coded**, so translating a joke literally usually kills it; explaining it always does (the classic warning — a joke explained is a joke dead).

## 3. Reading Humorous Texts — The Analyst's Method

### 3.1 Locate the mechanism before you laugh

For any set passage, ask in order: What is the **target** (a person, a vice, the narrator himself)? What is the **device** (irony, exaggeration, understatement, pun)? Where is the **turn** — the moment the second frame appears? An answer that names device, target and turn is an analysis; one that says "it is very funny" is a review.

### 3.2 The devices that carry written comedy

- **Exaggeration (hyperbole):** "I was so nervous I could have buttered the ceiling with my fingertips."
- **Understatement (litotes):** after a cyclone — "The weather has turned slightly breezy."
- **Rule of three:** two ordinary items, then the odd one — "he packed his books, his pens, and his fear of mathematics."
- **Simile with mismatched registers:** "The exam hall was as silent as a bank during a robbery."
- **Anticlimax:** a grand build-up dropped onto a mundane landing — "He fought bravely for justice, honour and the last piece of cake."

### 3.3 Tone: laughing with, not at

Distinguish affectionate humour (the writer is inside the group being teased) from contemptuous humour (the writer is outside, punching down). The same incident — a politician losing his shoe — can be written warmly or cruelly; tone words in the passage (*fondly, poor man, our heroic fool*) are the evidence. NEB questions on tone are really asking for this distinction with a quotation.

## 4. Writing Humour — Craft, Not Chance

### 4.1 The comic sentence: setup, then surprise

Humour in writing is architecture: the setup builds one expectation in plain language, the punchline swaps the frame in as few words as possible — brevity at the turn is law ("I finally got eight hours of sleep. Four at a time."). Keep the surprise word at the end of the sentence; anything after a punchline is anti-climax in the wrong sense.

### 4.2 Exaggerate the true, not the invented

The best student comedy exaggerates a real, shared experience one step past sense: exam invigilators who patrol like border guards, the queue for the water cooler at break, a mother's ability to detect an untidy room through a closed door. Shared recognition — "it's true, we all do that" — is what earns the laugh; invented absurdity earns none.

### 4.3 Keep the essay honest underneath

Even a humorous essay needs a spine: the story of the disastrous picnic is also about optimism, or family, or rain. Write the spine first, add the comedy in the verbs and details. Examiners reward essays that are funny *and* about something — the humour is the vehicle, never the cargo.

## 5. Master Comparison — Satire versus Sarcasm versus Irony (the NEB classic)

| Basis | Irony | Sarcasm | Satire |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Core move | say the opposite of what is meant | irony aimed at a person | irony organised against a vice or institution |
| Target | situations, fate, oneself | usually an individual present | society's follies: greed, hypocrisy, corruption |
| Tone | can be gentle or bitter | biting, personal | mock-serious, public-spirited |
| Aim | wit, insight | to wound or score | to expose and reform |
| Presence of the victim | not required | required, and feels it | the powerful, safely absent |
| Example | "Lovely weather" in a downpour | "Nice of you to finally join us." | a mock awards ceremony for bribe-taking officials |
| Risk | misunderstood literally | damages relationships | misunderstood as endorsement if too deadpan |
| In exams | identify the gap between said and meant | identify the bite and its aim | identify the vice under the mock praise |

## 6. Conceptual Relationships

- **Unit 1 → here:** analysing humour IS critical thinking with a smile — device, target, turn is claim–evidence–reasoning wearing a party hat.
- **Here → Unit 8 (culture):** what a society laughs at is a census of its values; humour is culture's quickest X-ray.
- **Here → Unit 20 (power and politics):** satire is the citizen's safest weapon against the powerful — the court jester's licence survives in the political cartoon.
- **Here → writing units:** narrative tasks gain a band when one comic device appears with control; the rule of three and anticlimax transfer directly.

## 7. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 7.1 The recurring question patterns

1. **"What makes the passage humorous?" (4 marks)** — name two devices with quoted evidence and one line on where each turn happens; never merely retell the joke.
2. **"Distinguish irony and sarcasm" (2 marks)** — definition plus the target test: irony plays with situations; sarcasm plays with people.
3. **Narrative with humour (6–8 marks):** "A funny incident I cannot forget" — setup-turn structure per paragraph, exaggerate one true detail, land the spine in the last line.
4. **Short answer (2 marks):** "Why is humour called a social lubricant?" — it eases tension, builds bonds, allows criticism to be heard where direct words would be refused.

### 7.2 A worked miniature (analysis sentence)

"The writer's pride survives every mishap untouched: he calls the sinking canoe 'an unconventional ferry schedule' and his soaked files 'lightly laminated' — the understatement is the joke, and the target is not the river but his own refusal to admit defeat." — device named, quotation given, target identified: three marks in two sentences.

### 7.3 Time strategy

For "why is it funny" questions, hunt first for the opposites — formal words in informal scenes, grand words for small things, praise that cannot be sincere. One quoted phrase per device is enough evidence; quoting entire paragraphs wastes time and shows nothing.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Name the humour device precisely: irony, pun, hyperbole, situational comedy — precision of device + the quoted instance is the full-mark pair.
Trick 2: 'Why is this funny?' answers must explain the INCONGRUITY (what we expected vs what happened) — expectation violation is the theory to cite.
practiceQuestions: Q. What makes the situation in the text humorous? (2 marks) — the gap between expectation and outcome; cite the moment.
Q. Identify one example of irony in the text. (2 marks) — quote the line and explain the intended vs actual meaning.
keyPoints: Identify humour types: situational, verbal, irony — name the type then explain.
Humour often carries social criticism; state what is being mocked.
